description: How the nervous system, reflex arcs, synapses, brain and eye coordinate responses.
hero_image_caption: A branching motor neurone, the specialised cell that carries signals from the spinal cord to muscles.
content_html:
Structure of the Nervous System

The human nervous system allows the body to detect changes in the environment (stimuli) and produce rapid, coordinated responses. It consists of the central nervous system (CNS) — the brain and spinal cord — and the peripheral nervous system — nerves that connect the CNS to receptors and effectors throughout the body (B3.1a).

The pathway for any nervous response follows a clear sequence: stimulus → sensory receptor → sensory neurone → CNS (relay neurone) → motor neurone → effector → response.

Key Fact

The nervous pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in CNS) → motor neurone → effector → response. The CNS (brain and spinal cord) processes information and coordinates the response.

Neurones and Their Structure

There are three types of neurone. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. Relay neurones are found within the CNS and link sensory neurones to motor neurones. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands).

Both sensory and motor neurones share common structural features: a cell body containing the nucleus, short dendrites that receive incoming impulses, and a long axon that carries the electrical impulse away from the cell body. In motor neurones the long axon runs directly from the spinal cord to the effector. In sensory neurones a long dendron connects the receptor to the cell body, with a shorter axon entering the CNS. The axon is often surrounded by a myelin sheath, which insulates the axon and greatly increases the speed of impulse transmission.

Synapses

Where two neurones meet there is a tiny gap called a synapse. An electrical impulse cannot cross this gap directly. Instead, when an impulse arrives at the end of the pre-synaptic neurone, neurotransmitters are released from vesicles into the synaptic cleft. These chemicals diffuse across the gap and bind to specific receptors on the post-synaptic neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse that continues the pathway.

Synapses ensure impulses travel in one direction only, because neurotransmitters are released from one side and receptors are only present on the other. They also allow one neurone to connect with several others simultaneously, enabling complex coordination throughout the nervous system (B3.1b).

A reflex arc is the pathway that produces a rapid, automatic, protective response without conscious thought (B3.1c). The pathway goes: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector. Crucially, the signal passes through the spinal cord rather than the brain, making the response faster than a voluntary reaction.

For example, when your fingertip touches something sharp: pain receptors detect the stimulus → a sensory neurone carries the impulse to the spinal cord → a relay neurone connects directly to a motor neurone → the motor neurone stimulates arm muscles to contract → the hand is withdrawn. This protects the body from harm before conscious awareness of pain. Other reflex examples include the pupil reflex (pupils constrict in bright light) and the knee-jerk reflex.

Key Fact

Reflex arcs produce rapid, automatic responses that bypass the brain and pass through the spinal cord instead. This makes reflexes faster than voluntary responses and protects the body from injury before conscious thought.

The ruler drop test is a simple practical used to measure voluntary reaction time (B3.1c practical context, PAG B6). One person holds a ruler vertically at the 0 cm mark; the subject places their thumb and finger at the base without touching it. When the ruler is released without warning, the subject catches it as quickly as possible. The shorter the distance fallen, the faster the reaction time.

To improve reliability: repeat at least five times, discard anomalous results, and calculate a mean. Variables that could affect results include caffeine, fatigue, distractions and practice. This experiment measures a voluntary response rather than a true reflex — the information passes through the brain (visual cortex → motor cortex) rather than being processed in the spinal cord.

The Brain

The brain is the main coordination centre of the nervous system. It contains billions of neurones connected by synapses. Three regions are particularly important to know (B3.1d):

Cerebral cortex — the highly folded outer layer of the brain responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory, language and personality. The folding greatly increases surface area, allowing more neurones to be packed in. Different regions of the cortex are specialised — for example, the visual cortex processes information from the eyes, and the motor cortex controls voluntary muscle movements.

Cerebellum — located at the back of the brain. It coordinates balance, fine motor control and smooth, precise movements. Damage to the cerebellum results in loss of coordination and unsteady movement.

Medulla oblongata — at the base of the brain where it connects to the spinal cord. It controls involuntary, life-sustaining processes such as breathing rate, heart rate and swallowing. Because these functions are automatic, the medulla keeps them running without conscious thought.

Our understanding of brain function comes from several sources: studying patients with brain injuries, using electroencephalography (EEG) to record electrical activity, and modern MRI scanning to map active brain regions. However, the brain is enormously complex — many functions involve multiple regions working together, and some functions remain poorly understood. This makes treating brain disorders challenging.

The Eye

The eye is a complex sensory receptor for light (B3.1d). The key structures to know are: the cornea (refracts light), the iris (controls pupil size and therefore light entering), the lens (focuses light onto the retina), and the retina (converts light into electrical impulses via rod and cone photoreceptors). Impulses travel to the brain via the optic nerve.

Accommodation is the ability of the eye to focus on objects at different distances by changing the shape of the lens. To focus on a near object: the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken, and the lens becomes fatter (more curved) to refract light more strongly. To focus on a distant object: the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments pull taut, and the lens becomes thinner (less curved), refracting light less.

Myopia (short-sightedness): distant objects appear blurred because the eyeball is too long or the lens too curved, causing light to focus in front of the retina. Corrected with a concave (diverging) lens. Hyperopia (long-sightedness): near objects are blurred because the eyeball is too short or lens too flat, causing light to focus behind the retina. Corrected with a convex (converging) lens. Both can now also be corrected with laser eye surgery, which reshapes the cornea.
exam_tip_html: Questions about the reflex arc often ask you to explain why it is faster than a voluntary response — the key point is that the signal does not travel to the brain, so fewer synapses are crossed and the pathway is shorter. For brain region questions, link each region to a specific function: cerebral cortex → consciousness and language; cerebellum → coordination; medulla → breathing and heart rate. For the eye, make sure you can distinguish between accommodation (ciliary muscles and lens shape changes) and the pupil reflex (iris muscles). ‘Explain’ questions need the mechanism, not just the outcome.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The nervous system coordinates responses via the pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (CNS) → motor neurone → effector. Synapses use neurotransmitters to pass signals in one direction only.
  • Reflex arcs bypass the brain and pass through the spinal cord, making them faster and protective. Three key brain regions: cerebral cortex (consciousness), cerebellum (coordination), medulla (heartbeat and breathing).
  • The eye focuses light via accommodation — the lens shape is controlled by ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments. Myopia (too curved/long eye) is corrected by concave lenses; hyperopia (too flat/short eye) by convex lenses.

practice_questions.text: Name the type of neurone that carries impulses from the CNS to an effector.
Describe what happens at a synapse when a nerve impulse reaches the end of a neurone.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Neurotransmitters are released from vesicles into the synaptic cleft (1); they diffuse across the gap and bind to specific receptor molecules on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse (1). Emerging: Vague reference to 'chemicals crossing the gap' without naming neurotransmitters or explaining receptor binding.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a reflex response is faster than a voluntary response to the same stimulus.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The reflex arc passes through the spinal cord rather than the brain (1), so the pathway is shorter with fewer synapses to cross (1), meaning the impulse reaches the effector more quickly (1). Secure: Two of the three points clearly linked. Developing: States reflexes are faster but gives no mechanistic explanation. Emerging: Vague or incorrect — e.g. 'the muscles react on their own'.

practice_questions.text: A student holds a ruler vertically and releases it unexpectedly. The subject's hand moves 0.12 m before catching it. Use the equation \(t = \sqrt{\frac{2d}{g}}\) where \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\) to calculate the reaction time. Show your working and give your answer to 2 significant figures.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Substitution correct — \(t = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 0.12}{9.8}}\) (1); correct calculation of \(\frac{0.24}{9.8} = 0.02449\) (1); square root taken correctly: \(t = 0.156...\) s (1); rounded correctly to 2 s.f.: 0.16 s with unit (1). Penalise missing unit or incorrect rounding.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the eye focuses on a nearby object. In your answer, refer to the ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments and the lens.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Ciliary muscles contract (1); suspensory ligaments slacken/go slack (1); lens becomes fatter/more curved, increasing refraction to focus light on the retina (1). Secure: Two points with correct logic. Developing: States 'lens changes shape' but does not describe the mechanism. Emerging: Confused — e.g. 'muscles relax so lens gets fatter'.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using reflex actions to protect the body. In your answer, consider speed of response, level of control and potential limitations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Reflexes are very rapid because they bypass the brain and use only spinal cord relay neurones, reducing the number of synapses crossed; this is advantageous in situations of immediate danger (touching heat, sharp objects). Reflexes are involuntary — they cannot be easily overridden, which ensures a consistent protective response. However, the lack of conscious control can be a disadvantage: the response is fixed and cannot be modified based on context. Voluntary responses, though slower, allow the organism to assess danger and make a considered decision. A well-argued conclusion noting that reflexes are essential for survival but limited in scope. Secure: Four well-reasoned points. Developing: Two points with limited evaluation. Emerging: One point with no evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination of movement?
Which statement correctly describes the role of synapses?
options: They allow electrical impulses to jump directly between neurones
They ensure impulses travel in one direction using neurotransmitters
They speed up impulses by providing a short-circuit pathway
They connect the brain to the spinal cord

knowledge_checks.q: In a reflex arc, the signal passes through the _____ rather than the brain, making the response faster.
To focus on a near object, the ciliary muscles _____, causing the lens to become fatter.
Match each brain region to its function.
right: Controls breathing and heart rate automatically
Responsible for consciousness, language and memory

flashcard_questions.q: What is the correct order of the nervous pathway from stimulus to response?
flashcard_questions.a: Stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector → response

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of neurotransmitters at a synapse?
flashcard_questions.a: They diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new impulse

flashcard_questions.q: Why do reflex arcs bypass the brain?
flashcard_questions.a: To reduce pathway length and the number of synapses crossed, producing a faster protective response

flashcard_questions.q: What does the myelin sheath do?
flashcard_questions.a: Insulates the axon and speeds up the transmission of electrical impulses

flashcard_questions.q: Which brain region controls heartbeat and breathing rate?
Which brain region is responsible for consciousness, memory and language?
What happens to the lens when focusing on a close object?
flashcard_questions.a: Ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken, and the lens becomes fatter (more curved)

flashcard_questions.q: What vision defect does a concave lens correct, and what causes it?
flashcard_questions.a: Myopia — the eyeball is too long or lens too curved, so light focuses in front of the retina
The ability of the eye to change lens shape to focus on objects at different distances

flashcard_questions.q: Name the layer at the back of the eye that contains photoreceptors.
What type of response does a reflex arc produce?
flashcard_questions.a: A rapid, automatic, involuntary protective response

flashcard_questions.q: State one difference between a sensory neurone and a motor neurone.
flashcard_questions.a: Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS; motor neurones carry impulses from CNS to effectors

glossary_terms.definition: The organ system consisting of the brain, spinal cord and nerves that detects stimuli and coordinates the body's responses.
Specialised cells that detect stimuli such as light, sound, temperature, pressure or chemicals and convert them into electrical impulses.
An organ that carries out a response to a nervous impulse, such as a muscle (which contracts) or a gland (which secretes a substance).
A nerve cell that transmits electrical impulses; types include sensory, relay and motor neurones.
A fatty, insulating layer around the axon of a neurone that speeds up the transmission of electrical impulses by preventing charge leakage.
The junction between two neurones where a chemical neurotransmitter is released from one neurone to trigger a new electrical impulse in the next.
The organ of the central nervous system that processes information from the senses and coordinates all voluntary and involuntary responses.
The tough, transparent outer layer at the front of the eye that refracts light as it enters.
The flexible, transparent disc behind the iris that changes shape to focus light onto the retina.
The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye containing rod and cone photoreceptor cells that convert light into electrical impulses.
The process by which the lens changes shape to focus light from objects at different distances onto the retina.
